• Common name: Creeping Jenny
  • Difficulty: Easy
  • Lighting: Moderate
  • pH: 6.0–8.0
  • GH: 4–16
  • Temperature: 15–30°C
  • Substrate: Any
  • Can be grown emersed: Yes
  • Growth rate: Moderate to fast
  • Placement: Midground and background
  • CO2: Optional
  • Propagation: Vegetative, by cuttings
  • Colour: Green

This plant is native to Europe (from southern Sweden down to Spain, east to Greece and the Caucasus) but has spread to many parts of the world. It is now naturalized in Asia, New Zealand, Australia (New South Wales), Canada and the eastern United States.

It is a floodplain-inhabiting species, usually found in wetlands, marshes, swamps, stream banks, roadsides, ditches, forest edges and other moist areas, from sea level up to about 1 km elevation.

It is not generally considered a submersed aquatic plant but adapts very well. In nature it dislikes deep water and can be found at depths up to about 0.5 m.

In an aquarium the plant grows upwards only, so given its size the minimum tank is about 40 litres. Tall tanks are better than long tanks.

In a paludarium it can quickly form a dense mat and occupy a larger area, so long tanks are better than tall ones.

It can live in aquatic or humid conditions. In aquariums it is used as a classic stem plant, planted along the sides in the midground or background.

Be ready to trim it often, since growth is medium to fast. Once established, it may need propagation or trimming within a few weeks. Do not let it reach the surface, or it may form a big tangled mass. Start trimming when it is 10–15 cm from the surface; you can safely shorten it by half. Regular trimming prevents overcrowding and promotes bushier growth.

Planting

  • Remove the plant from its pot and carefully separate tangled roots.
  • Dig a small hole in the substrate and place the roots in it.
  • Cover the roots with substrate so they are firmly anchored.

Keep stems at least 5 cm apart.

Some aquarists try to use it as a carpet plant by planting it with the dry start method and flooding the tank once it has rooted in several places. Although the stems may stay horizontal at first, new shoots tend to grow upwards over time.

Common problems

  • Ugly roots: it develops a few adventitious (aerial) roots at the nodes. They cannot be avoided completely, only trimmed.
  • Leggy growth: when the stem reaches the surface, lower leaves may be shed. Trim it or place it behind driftwood or rocks to hide the bare stem.
  • Overgrowth: with high light, fertilization and CO2 it can fill the tank within a few months and needs regular trimming.
  • Rust and leaf spots: occur when kept emersed in too warm and humid conditions. Ensure proper spacing, good airflow and avoid overhead watering.

Temperature: it thrives in both cold (15°C) and warm (30°C) water. Growth is faster in warmer water, but leaves may be smaller.

pH: it grows in acidic or alkaline water; pH 6.0–8.0 is fine.

Hardness: it adapts to a wide range (4–16 GH).

Lighting: it prefers moderate to high light; full-spectrum light for 10–12 hours a day is generally suitable. It tolerates lower light, but growth is significantly slower.

Flow: not mandatory, but gentle water movement is optimal, helping distribute nutrients and oxygen and preventing debris build-up on leaves and stems.

Substrate: undemanding, since it mainly absorbs nutrients from the water. Almost any substrate works, though a finer texture helps rooting and anchoring.

CO2 and fertilization: CO2 is optional but significantly boosts growth. Regular fertilization is needed, although in a densely stocked tank waste from fish and snails may substitute under some conditions. If keeping shrimp, note that high CO2 and copper (found in many fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to them.

Emersed propagation: by stolon — as the stem extends horizontally, new roots form at the nodes, creating new plants. The plant also produces seeds, but this is rather rare.

Submersed propagation: by stem cuttings.

  • Take a healthy cutting with several leaves and nodes.
  • Cut it.
  • Remove leaves from the lower part and plant it in the substrate.

Tip: if the cutting keeps floating, let it float in the aquarium for 1–2 weeks until roots start growing from the nodes, then plant it.

Description

A perennial plant with prostrate stems. It can be grown partly emersed (paludarium) or fully submersed. In aquariums it can exceed 50 cm in height; in a paludarium the stems creep horizontally into leafy mats. Stems have 4 wings. Leaves are smooth, opposite, oval to round, 10–25 mm long and wide, dark green above and lighter below. Yellow flowers with usually 5 petals appear above the water. The plant is self-fertile and flowers May to August.

Benefits

  • Attractive yellow flowers for ornamental use.
  • Not a preferred food of fish, so it suits tanks where fish damage plants.
  • Provides a grazing surface for shrimp.
  • Absorbs nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
  • Forms thick bushes giving shrimp and fry hiding places.

Quarantine

Plants collected from nearby waters may introduce parasites (leeches, pest snails, dragonfly and damselfly nymphs). Plants from shops or greenhouses may carry pesticide residues that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates. Always quarantine the plant.

Note: in 2010 the New York Invasive Species Council recommended prohibiting this species as a problematic invasive weed.
